title: The Bond That Made Nitrogen Scarce
topic: nitrogen fixation and industrial ammonia synthesis
paragraphs: Roughly seventy eight percent of every breath a person takes is nitrogen, and yet nitrogen is the nutrient that most often decides how much a field can yield.
A plant can stand in an ocean of the element it needs and still go hungry for it.
Sorting that out took chemistry most of a century, and the process that finally managed it now ranks among the largest industrial consumers of energy on the planet.
The line from one chemical bond to a coastal dead zone is shorter than it looks.
Begin with the bond.
Two nitrogen atoms in the air are held by a triple bond, three shared pairs of electrons, and pulling that bond apart costs roughly nine hundred and forty five kilojoules per mole.
Few bonds in ordinary chemistry are stronger.
The molecule is also symmetrical from end to end, with no partially positive or partially negative region where a reagent could get a grip.
Nitrogen gas is therefore not unreactive because reacting is impossible.
Most of its reactions release energy overall.
It is unreactive because the first step, breaking that bond, sits behind a wall almost nothing at ordinary temperatures can climb.
That distinction, between a reaction that cannot happen and a reaction that will not start, runs through the whole subject.
Lightning supplies enough local energy to force the issue, tearing nitrogen and oxygen apart and letting them recombine into oxides that rain out as nitrate.
Measured against what the world's crops pull out of the soil each season, that whole natural supply is a rounding error.
The route that mattered for most of life's history is biological.
A scattered set of bacteria and archaea, called diazotrophs, carry an enzyme named nitrogenase that does at ordinary temperature and pressure what industry still cannot do without extreme conditions.
At its center sits a cluster of iron and molybdenum atoms that grips the nitrogen molecule and feeds electrons into it one at a time, weakening the bond in stages rather than snapping it in one blow.
The accounting is brutal.
Reducing one molecule of nitrogen gas to two molecules of ammonia consumes sixteen molecules of ATP, the cell's energy currency.
Which sets up the central difficulty of biological fixation.
Sixteen ATP is an enormous bill, and the cheapest way any cell has to pay it is aerobic respiration, which requires oxygen.
Yet oxygen poisons nitrogenase.
Not in the mild, reversible way a competing molecule slows an enzyme and then lets go: oxygen attacks the exposed metal cluster and wrecks it, and the cell has to build a replacement from scratch.
A fixing organism therefore needs oxygen present in one compartment and absent in another, a few micrometers apart.
Everything interesting about the biology follows from that one conflict.
Different lineages settled it differently.

Filamentous cyanobacteria build heterocysts, thick walled cells that slow gas entry and have the oxygen producing half of their photosynthetic machinery dismantled, so the fixing cell makes none of the gas that would destroy its enzyme.
Legumes, the family that includes soybeans, peas and clover, strike a bargain with soil bacteria instead.
The plant grows a nodule on its root, houses the bacteria inside, and floods it with leghemoglobin, an oxygen binding protein like the one that reddens blood.

Leghemoglobin does something more elegant than shutting oxygen out: it holds free oxygen in the nodule at a vanishingly low concentration while still ferrying a steady supply to the bacterial respiratory chain, so the bill gets paid and the enzyme survives.
Farmers exploited the arrangement for thousands of years with no idea it existed.
Rotating a cereal with a legume, or plowing a stand of clover back into the ground, restored something to a tired field.

The name for the practice arrived long before the name for the mechanism, and for most of agricultural history the usable nitrogen supply was capped by whatever those bacteria, plus manure and a little lightning, happened to deliver.
By the nineteenth century that cap was being felt.
European agriculture leaned on seabird guano shipped from the Peruvian coast and on nitrate mined in the Chilean desert, deposits that were rich, concentrated and finite.

In 1898 the president of the British Association for the Advancement of Science gave his annual address over to the arithmetic: wheat consumption was climbing, the nitrate beds would not last, and the shortfall would have to be met by pulling nitrogen out of the air.
Within fifteen years the chemists had answered him.
Fritz Haber demonstrated the reaction on a laboratory bench in 1909, coaxing a slow drip of ammonia out of nitrogen and hydrogen passed over a heated catalyst.

Carl Bosch and his colleagues at a German chemical firm then spent four years turning that result into a factory, which meant inventing steel vessels that would not fail under sustained pressure and screening thousands of catalysts for one both active and affordable.
The first full scale works opened in 1913.
The modern version still runs near four hundred to five hundred degrees Celsius and one hundred and fifty to three hundred atmospheres, and it still uses iron.
Those conditions are not arbitrary.
Combining nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia gives off heat, and it turns four molecules of gas into two.
Both facts argue for running the reaction cold and squeezed, since low temperature favors a heat releasing product and high pressure favors the side with fewer gas molecules.
The trouble is that a low temperature also means a bond nothing wants to break breaks even more slowly.
So the conditions are a deliberate compromise.

Engineers accept a hotter reactor than equilibrium would prefer, since a small share of a fast reaction beats a large share of one that never finishes, then raise the pressure to claw back some lost yield.
The catalyst is the other half of the bargain, and it acts on the rate alone.
It cannot move where equilibrium lies; it only lowers the barrier to getting there.
An iron surface pulls the nitrogen molecule down flat and splits it into separate atoms held on the metal, after which hydrogen adds one atom at a time.
The working material is iron promoted with small quantities of potassium and aluminum oxides, additives that carry out no reaction themselves but keep the iron surface open and lift its activity.
Even so, one pass converts only ten to twenty percent of the feed, so the unreacted gas is cooled, stripped of its ammonia, and sent around again.
The consequences were not subtle.
Nitrogen stopped being something a farm had to grow or a company had to mine and became something a factory could make from air, water and fuel.

World population stood near one and a half billion in 1900 and is near eight billion now, and by common estimate close to half the nitrogen in the protein of a person alive today entered the food chain through an ammonia reactor rather than a root nodule.
It is tempting to stop there and file the process under unambiguous triumph, and that reading is too clean.
The trouble is not the reaction, which is remarkably good at what it does.
The trouble is everything downstream of the reactor.
Across the world's farms, well under half of the nitrogen applied to a field ends up inside the harvested crop.
The rest is lost, and those losses are not a rounding error.
A technology can be an extraordinary piece of chemistry and a careless piece of plumbing at once, and the honest description of synthetic nitrogen is that it is both.
The leaking has a chemical reason.
Soil particles carry a net negative charge, so positively charged ammonium is held in place by plain attraction.
Soil bacteria, though, convert ammonium to nitrate within days, and nitrate is negative.
The soil repels it, and the next heavy rain carries it past the roots into groundwater or sideways into a ditch and a river.
Some of the surplus leaves as nitrous oxide instead, a gas that traps roughly three hundred times as much heat per molecule as carbon dioxide and that has become a leading threat to the ozone layer.
What the nitrate does at the coast follows a sequence.
River water arrives loaded with nutrients and fertilizes a bloom of algae at the surface.
The algae grow, they die, and they sink.
Bacteria near the bottom decompose the falling material and consume dissolved oxygen as they work.
Meanwhile the warm fresh river water floats on colder, saltier seawater in a layer that resists mixing, so oxygen from the surface cannot get down to replace what the bacteria are using.
The bottom water goes hypoxic.
Fish that can swim leave; crabs, clams and worms that cannot, die.
Each summer the hypoxic zone at the mouth of the Mississippi covers several thousand square miles.
The energy side of the ledger is just as awkward.
The hydrogen for ammonia is stripped out of natural gas with steam, so most of the world's fertilizer begins as fossil carbon and releases carbon dioxide before it ever reaches a field.
Ammonia synthesis accounts for somewhere between one and two percent of global energy use and a comparable share of industrial carbon emissions.
That is a large bill for one reaction, and not one that can simply be refused, because the alternative to the fertilizer is not a cleaner fertilizer but a great deal less food.
Which is why the promising work aims at the losses, not the reaction.
Applying fertilizer in several small doses timed to the crop's demand, instead of one heavy dose in spring, leaves less nitrate sitting in wet soil with nothing to absorb it.
Compounds that slow the bacterial conversion of ammonium to nitrate buy the roots more time.
Cover crops take up leftover nitrogen through the winter, and legume rotations supply part of the need biologically.
Making the hydrogen by splitting water with renewable electricity would address the fuel side without touching the chemistry.
None of it repeals the triple bond.
That bond is why nitrogen was scarce and why the remedy is expensive, and that much has not changed since 1909.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, nitrogen gas in the air resists reacting mainly because
choices: its reactions with other elements take in more energy than they give off
breaking the bond between its two atoms demands an enormous first push
one end of the molecule is partially negative and pushes reagents away
it is far too dilute in the atmosphere for reactions to get started
its two atoms share two pairs of electrons instead of three

proof.quote: breaking that bond, sits behind a wall almost nothing at ordinary temperatures can climb
Most of its reactions release energy overall.
no partially positive or partially negative region

questions.why: Paragraph 2 makes the point directly. Most nitrogen reactions release energy overall, so the block is not that reacting is impossible. The block is the first step, breaking a triple bond that costs roughly nine hundred forty five kilojoules per mole.
distractorNotes: The passage says the opposite, that most of nitrogen's reactions release energy overall.
Paragraph 2 calls the molecule symmetrical, with no partially positive or partially negative region at all.
Nitrogen is about seventy eight percent of the air, so being too dilute is not the problem.
A triple bond is three shared pairs rather than two, and that third pair is the whole difficulty.

questions.stem: Paragraph 4 states that turning one molecule of nitrogen gas into ammonia costs the cell
choices: two molecules of ATP, one for each ammonia made
eight molecules of ATP
sixteen molecules of ATP, but only in cells that lack oxygen
sixteen molecules of ATP
an amount of energy the passage treats as negligible

proof.quote: consumes sixteen molecules of ATP

questions.why: This is a straight number check against paragraph 4. Reducing one nitrogen molecule to two ammonia molecules runs the cell sixteen ATP, which is why the passage calls the accounting brutal.
distractorNotes: The passage never ties the ATP count to the number of ammonia molecules made, and the real figure is far higher.
Eight is not the number given, and it would make the cost sound modest rather than brutal.
The number is right, but the passage attaches no oxygen condition to it; the oxygen problem arrives in the next paragraph.
Paragraph 4 calls the accounting brutal, which is the opposite of negligible.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 6, leghemoglobin serves the root nodule by
choices: sealing the nodule so that no oxygen at all can get in
thickening the nodule wall so that gases enter slowly
holding free oxygen very low while still feeding oxygen to the bacteria
converting ammonium into nitrate that the plant can absorb
supplying the electrons that nitrogenase pushes into the nitrogen molecule

proof.quote: holds free oxygen in the nodule at a vanishingly low concentration while still ferrying
more elegant than shutting oxygen out

questions.why: Paragraph 6 draws the distinction for you. Leghemoglobin does something more elegant than shutting oxygen out: it keeps free oxygen vanishingly low in the nodule while still ferrying a steady supply to the bacteria so they can pay the ATP bill.
distractorNotes: This is the reading the paragraph specifically rules out, since the bacteria still need oxygen to make their ATP.
That is the heterocyst solution used by cyanobacteria, not what leghemoglobin does.
Soil bacteria make that conversion in paragraph 14, out in the field rather than inside the nodule.
Paragraph 6 gives leghemoglobin an oxygen handling job only, and says nothing about where the electrons come from.

questions.stem: Paragraph 11 reports that one pass of the feed gas through the reactor
choices: turns nearly all of the nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia
converts only about ten to twenty percent of it
ruins the iron catalyst, which then has to be replaced
shifts the position of equilibrium toward more ammonia
removes any need for high pressure later on

proof.quote: one pass converts only ten to twenty percent of the feed

questions.why: Paragraph 11 gives the figure at the end. A single pass converts only ten to twenty percent of the feed, which is why the leftover gas is cooled, stripped of its ammonia and sent around again.
distractorNotes: If that were true there would be no reason to recycle the leftover gas, which the paragraph says is standard.
The passage never says the catalyst is used up; it says the catalyst lowers the barrier to reaction.
Paragraph 11 states plainly that a catalyst cannot move where equilibrium lies, only how fast the reaction gets there.
High pressure is still part of the design in paragraph 10, and the low conversion is exactly why it is needed.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 15, oxygen fails to reach the bottom water near the river mouth because
choices: the algae at the surface use it up before any of it can sink
nitrate binds it chemically and pulls it out of solution
the bacteria near the bottom give off nitrous oxide in place of oxygen
wind stirs the surface layer downward only during winter
warm fresh water floats on colder salty water and resists mixing

proof.quote: floats on colder, saltier seawater in a layer that resists mixing

questions.why: Paragraph 15 puts the layering in the middle of the sequence. Warm fresh river water sits on colder, saltier seawater, and that boundary keeps surface oxygen from getting down to replace what the bacteria are using.
distractorNotes: The algae fuel the problem by dying and sinking, and the oxygen is consumed by bacteria on the bottom.
Nitrate in this passage feeds the algal bloom, and no chemical binding of oxygen is described.
Nitrous oxide appears in paragraph 14 as a loss from farm soil, not as something released on the sea floor.
The passage never mentions wind or a winter cycle, so this comes from outside the text.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 5, "poisons" most nearly means
choices: makes unfit to eat
slows for a while and then lets go
damages beyond repair
coats with a trace impurity
makes unpleasant to the taste

proof.quote: oxygen attacks the exposed metal cluster and wrecks it
Not in the mild, reversible way

questions.why: Paragraph 5 defines the word by contrast. Oxygen does not slow nitrogenase the way a competing molecule does and then release it; it wrecks the metal cluster so thoroughly that the cell has to build a new one.
distractorNotes: That is the everyday sense of the word, and nothing in this sentence is being eaten.
The paragraph names that reversible behavior only in order to say this is not it.
The passage describes real destruction of the metal cluster, not a film or a contaminant.
Taste plays no part here, since the subject is an enzyme being put out of action.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 11, "promoted" most nearly means
choices: advertised to possible buyers
moved up to a higher rank
heated thoroughly before use
made more active by added substances
purified until no other element remains on the surface

proof.quote: keep the iron surface open and lift its activity

questions.why: The sentence explains itself in paragraph 11. The iron carries small amounts of potassium and aluminum oxides, additives that run no reaction of their own but keep the surface open and lift the iron's activity.
distractorNotes: That is the marketing sense of the word, which has no place in a description of a catalyst surface.
Rank belongs to people and jobs, while the paragraph is describing what additives do to a metal.
Heating is set by the operating temperature in paragraph 9, not by the word describing the additives.
The additives are deliberately present, so the iron is not being cleaned of everything else.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which conclusion about a fertilizer that stayed in the ammonium form longer than usual?
choices: It would wash out of the soil more easily during a heavy rain
It would linger in the soil and reach the water less readily
It would stop soil bacteria from growing anywhere near the roots
It would remove the need to fertilize that field in later seasons
It would keep nitrous oxide from forming under any conditions

proof.quote: positively charged ammonium is held in place by plain attraction
the next heavy rain carries it past the roots into groundwater
buy the roots more time

questions.why: Paragraph 14 supplies both halves. Soil particles are negatively charged, so positive ammonium is held in place, while nitrate is negative and gets repelled and carried off. Ammonium that lingers is ammonium that stays put.
distractorNotes: That is the behavior of nitrate, the negatively charged form the soil pushes away.
Nothing in the passage says ammonium harms bacteria; paragraph 14 says bacteria convert it within days.
The passage never claims one application could carry a field through later seasons.
Paragraph 17 describes slowing that conversion, which is not the same as shutting off nitrous oxide entirely.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from paragraph 16 that giving up synthetic fertilizer altogether would
choices: leave the world with a great deal less food
have little effect on the food supply, since biology could take over at once
make the nitrogen in the air easier for crops to use directly
cut global energy use roughly in half
raise the share of applied nitrogen that crops take up

proof.quote: not a cleaner fertilizer but a great deal less food

questions.why: Paragraph 16 closes on exactly this point. The bill for ammonia synthesis is large, but it cannot simply be refused, because the alternative to the fertilizer is not a cleaner fertilizer but a great deal less food.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 says close to half the nitrogen in human protein comes through the reactor, so the effect would be large.
Nothing about the triple bond changes, and paragraph 17 says none of the remedies repeal it.
The passage puts ammonia synthesis at one to two percent of global energy use, not half.
Uptake depends on how nitrate behaves in soil, and closing the factory would not change that chemistry.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Biological fixation in root nodules is more efficient than the industrial process and could replace it if farmers planted more legumes
Coastal dead zones are the single most serious environmental problem the world now faces
An unusually stable bond kept nitrogen scarce until industry learned to break it, a fix that feeds billions and leaks badly
Early twentieth century chemists solved a problem that farmers had already solved by rotating their fields
Ammonia synthesis should be shut down because its energy cost outweighs what it provides

proof.quote: The line from one chemical bond to a coastal dead zone is shorter
close to half the nitrogen in the protein of a person alive today
an extraordinary piece of chemistry and a careless piece of plumbing at once
That bond is why nitrogen was scarce and why the remedy is expensive

questions.why: The passage runs from the strength of the triple bond, through the biological and industrial ways around it, to the food it produces and the nitrogen that escapes. Paragraph 13 states the balanced verdict: extraordinary chemistry, careless plumbing.
distractorNotes: The passage never ranks the two for efficiency, and paragraph 16 says removing the factory would mean far less food.
Dead zones get one paragraph as a consequence, and no claim is made about their rank among world problems.
Farmers raised the ceiling without removing it, since paragraph 7 says the supply stayed capped by what the bacteria delivered.
Paragraph 16 makes the opposite point, that this particular bill cannot simply be refused.

choices: show two different ways organisms settle the conflict raised just before it
prove that legumes fix more nitrogen than cyanobacteria do
explain why farmers began rotating cereal crops with legumes in the first place
describe the color of a healthy root nodule
argue that biological fixation ought to replace industrial ammonia

proof.quote: Everything interesting about the biology follows from that one conflict.
Different lineages settled it differently.
with no idea it existed

questions.why: Paragraph 5 ends by saying everything interesting in the biology follows from one conflict, oxygen needed and oxygen fatal. Paragraph 6 then lays out two answers to it, the heterocyst and the nodule.
distractorNotes: The paragraph sets the two strategies side by side without comparing how much nitrogen either one fixes.
Crop rotation is taken up in the next paragraph, while paragraph 6 stays on the biology.
Nodule color is never mentioned, and a detail that small could not carry a paragraph.
The author never makes that argument, and paragraph 16 says the industrial supply cannot simply be given up.

questions.stem: Which best describes the way the passage is organized?
choices: a list of the scientists who worked on nitrogen, in the order they worked
a comparison of two industrial processes that compete with each other today
a claim, a long objection raised against it, and a return to the claim unchanged
a series of regional case studies of how fertilizer is used
one chemical obstacle, its two answers, and the cost of the industrial one

proof.quote: Begin with the bond.
The route that mattered for most of life's history is biological.
Within fifteen years the chemists had answered him.
The trouble is everything downstream of the reactor.

questions.why: The passage opens on the triple bond in paragraph 2, works through biology in paragraphs 4 to 7 and industry in paragraphs 8 to 12, and spends paragraphs 13 to 17 on what the industrial answer costs.
distractorNotes: Two chemists are named in passing, but the passage is built around a chemical problem rather than around people.
Only one industrial process is described, and nothing is set against it as a competitor.
The author does not return to the opening verdict unchanged, since paragraph 13 revises it on purpose.
No region is studied on its own, and the Mississippi appears once as an example of a general pattern.

questions.stem: In paragraph 13, the author's attitude toward treating synthetic nitrogen as an unqualified success is best described as
choices: fully in agreement with it
dismissive of the chemistry behind the process
alarmed enough to call for the process to be shut down
unwilling to accept it without naming what the process loses
indifferent to what happens to the nitrogen after it is spread

proof.quote: that reading is too clean
the honest description of synthetic nitrogen is that it is both
remarkably good at what it does

questions.why: Paragraph 13 calls the triumphant reading too clean, then supplies the missing half, that well under half of applied nitrogen reaches the crop. The verdict at the end is both, not either.
distractorNotes: The paragraph opens by calling that reading too clean, which is a refusal rather than agreement.
The reaction is called remarkably good at what it does, so the chemistry is not what draws criticism.
No shutdown is called for anywhere, and paragraph 16 says the fertilizer cannot simply be refused.
Where the nitrogen goes afterward is the whole subject of the paragraph, so indifference does not fit.

questions.stem: The author's attitude in paragraph 17 toward the measures described there is best characterized as
choices: encouraged about the losses, clear that the chemistry is unchanged
confident that these steps will end coastal dead zones within a few years
doubtful that any of them is worth trying
irritated that farmers have not adopted them already
certain that they make the industrial process unnecessary

proof.quote: the promising work aims at the losses, not the reaction
None of it repeals the triple bond.

questions.why: Paragraph 17 lists measures that all aim at the losses, which is a hopeful list, and then closes by saying none of it repeals the triple bond. Positive about the plumbing, honest about the chemistry.
distractorNotes: No timeline is offered, and the closing sentences hold back from promising a cure.
The paragraph calls this the promising work, which is the opposite of doubt.
Farmers are never faulted here, since the paragraph describes practices rather than blaming anyone.
Paragraph 16 says the fertilizer cannot simply be given up, so these measures work alongside the process.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements about biological nitrogen fixation EXCEPT:
choices: It runs at ordinary temperature and pressure.
It costs the cell a large amount of energy.
Oxygen can wreck the enzyme that carries it out.
Legumes shelter the bacteria that carry it out inside nodules grown on their roots.
It now supplies most of the nitrogen used by the world's crops.

proof.quote: does at ordinary temperature and pressure
consumes sixteen molecules of ATP
oxygen attacks the exposed metal cluster and wrecks it
grows a nodule on its root, houses the bacteria inside
through an ammonia reactor rather than a root nodule
legume rotations supply part of the need biologically

questions.why: Paragraphs 4 through 7 support the other four statements. Paragraph 12 goes the other way on this one: by common estimate close to half the nitrogen in human protein now arrives through an ammonia reactor rather than a root nodule.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says nitrogenase does at ordinary temperature and pressure what industry needs extreme conditions to do.
Paragraph 4 puts the cost at sixteen ATP for one nitrogen molecule and calls the accounting brutal.
Paragraph 5 says oxygen attacks the metal cluster and wrecks it, leaving the cell to build a replacement.
Paragraph 6 describes the legume nodule, with the bacteria housed inside it.

questions.stem: In which paragraph would a reader find the source the hydrogen for ammonia is currently taken from?
choices: paragraph 4
paragraph 9
paragraph 11
paragraph 16
paragraph 17

proof.quote: The hydrogen for ammonia is stripped out of natural gas with steam
would address the fuel side

questions.why: Paragraph 16 is where the fuel side is handled. The hydrogen is stripped out of natural gas with steam, which is why the fertilizer begins as fossil carbon.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 is about the enzyme nitrogenase, not about where industrial hydrogen comes from.
Paragraph 9 covers the history and the operating conditions, and mentions hydrogen only as a feed gas.
Paragraph 11 explains what the iron catalyst does, without saying where the hydrogen is obtained.
Paragraph 17 offers splitting water as a possible future source, not the one in use now.
